still_true: Wegovy's US branded list price is still $1,349 a month, and almost nobody pays it.
The TrumpRx cash channel still operates, and oral Wegovy starting doses still cost $149 a month there.

The Medicare GLP-1 Bridge pilot has not been revived. Congress has not reopened the ~$41B CBO-scored permanent benefit, and Medicare reaches users only through diabetes, cardiovascular, kidney, sleep-apnoea and dementia-risk codes.

The September 2027 tri-agency guidance allowing up to 30% premium differentials tied to verified adherence still stands, and Illinois's ban on adherence-conditioned premiums is still the only state ban in force.
The suicidal-ideation warning is still off the labels.

population.note: FICTIONAL. Arithmetic: 25.6% ever-used minus 14.8% current leaves 10.8% of adults who used the drugs and are off now. 45% of ever-users have cycled, which is 11.5 points: ~8.1 points are current users on at least their second course (~55% of current users, up from 53% because most 2032 generic starts were lapsed users coming back) and ~3.4 points cycled and are off again (up from 1.8, mostly restarters who stopped after the Feb 2031 Novo disclosures and the Jul 2031 vision warning). The remaining ~7.4 points stopped once and never restarted. That fits one-year persistence near one-third and roughly 40% restarting within a year. Why ever-used rose only 0.1 point: gross first-time starts were ~1.7M over two years, with first-time starts in 2031 at their lowest since 2023. About 1.4M ever-users died in the window (an ageing pool of ~68M at ~1%/yr), and the adult denominator grew with mostly never-users. Age check: weights 0.20/0.33/0.24/0.23 × 8/15/23/12 ≈ 14.8. Income check: (18+15+11.5)/3 ≈ 14.8. About 14.8% of ~271M adults is ~40M users, down from ~47M. FICTIONAL payer mix: commercial ~30% (~12.0M, ~6.0M of them in conditional 'metabolic tracks'), Medicare ~22.5% (~9.0M, ~1.5M on the dementia-risk route), Medicaid ~7.5% (~3.0M), legitimate cash ~32.5% (~13.0M, ~5M of them on $39–69 generic semaglutide), gray market ~7.5% (~3.0M, down from 5.2M as generics undercut Indian vials). The decline is steepest in the top third (23 → 18): its members are the longest continuous users, the group the exocrine and vision findings hit hardest, and the most exposed to the Unpinned movement. The bottom third barely moved (12 → 11.5), but much of it moved from gray to legitimate supply. Off-drug: ~24% of adults have obesity and have never used a drug, and ~10.8% are former users, about two-thirds of them regaining. Pediatric: ~1.3% of under-18s, about 0.94M children: ~3.0% of 12–17s (~0.75M) and ~0.8% of 6–11s (~0.19M), split between generic liraglutide and, since Oct 2031, weekly semaglutide, now mostly generic.

access.public_coverage: Medicare still reaches users only through diabetes, CV, CKD, OSA and dementia-risk codes, all behind prior authorisation. ~9.0M users. FICTIONAL arithmetic: the dementia route (~1.5M on tirzepatide × ~$260 net × 12) ≈ $4.7B, plus all other codes (~7.5M × ~$158 blended net × 12, pulled down by generic semaglutide substitution from mid-2032) ≈ $14.2B, for ≈ $18.9B in gross Part D incretin spend in 2032, down from ~$29.7B. The FDA issued a complete response letter (Jul 2031) on Lilly's sNDA to extend the dementia claim to adults without CVD, so the route did not widen. Medicaid: the same 9 states cover weight-loss use, and existing preferred-drug-list rules moved them to generic semaglutide automatically. Two state programmes still condition coverage on adherence and BMI progress. ~3.0M users.
access.generic_rest_of_world: Indian generic semaglutide sells for $5–30 a month and Chinese tirzepatide analogues remain outside US-patent markets. Canadian generics are CAD 45–80. The US–India price gap has narrowed from ~40× to roughly 3–6× for semaglutide. Tirzepatide is still patent-protected in the US and EU, so Chinese analogue makers sell mainly to Southeast Asia, Latin America and the gray market.
access.note: FICTIONAL. Novo's US semaglutide compound patent expired in Dec 2031. A Nov 2031 settlement with Viatris, Teva, Sandoz and Hikma cleared the remaining pen and formulation patents. The FDA approved the first ANDAs, and generic injectable semaglutide launched in Jan 2032 alongside a Novo authorised generic. By Q3 2032 cash prices run $39–69 a month at Costco, Amazon Pharmacy, Cost Plus and Kroger. Branded Wegovy injectable on TrumpRx was cut to $199. Oral Wegovy starting doses stay $149 (oral semaglutide has no generic yet), and maintenance is $199–249. Zepbound holds at $279–329 cash. Retatrutide is $1,399 list or ~$549 through LillyDirect. MariTide is cut to $199 direct, and its clinic volume is falling as employers switch to cheaper generic weekly pens. Employer coverage rose from 36% to 41% because generics made coverage cheap, but ~90% of covering employers now attach conditions: generic-first step therapy, ≥5% weight loss at 6 months to continue, fill-data adherence, and premium differentials under the 2027 guidance. Access is now an income floor and a paperwork question, not a price question: $49 is affordable, but the eye exam, the micronutrient panel and the unpaid hour off are not free. Orals are ~38% of users, down from 45%. The remaining gray market is mostly 'research-grade' high-dose retatrutide and tirzepatide analogues.

on_market_classes: GLP-1 agonist, weekly injectable (semaglutide: Wegovy/Ozempic; generic semaglutide since Jan 2032)
GIP/GLP-1 dual agonist, weekly injectable (tirzepatide: Zepbound/Mounjaro)
GIP/GLP-1/glucagon triple agonist, weekly injectable (retatrutide; 12 mg high-dose approved Apr 2032)
GLP-1 agonist/GIP-receptor antagonist antibody conjugate, monthly injectable (MariTide)
GLP-1/amylin unimolecular agonist, weekly injectable (amycretin, approved Feb 2032)
GLP-1 agonist, daily oral peptide (Wegovy pill 25 mg; Rybelsus)
GLP-1 agonist, daily injectable (liraglutide: Saxenda, incl. generics)
indications_beyond_weight_and_diabetes: pediatric obesity ages 6–11 (liraglutide incl. generics, Jun 2029; weekly semaglutide, Oct 2031)
reduction of risk of all-cause dementia in adults with obesity and established CVD (tirzepatide); the extension to adults 60+ without CVD got a complete response letter in Jul 2031
mainstream_offlabel_uses: alcohol reduction via telehealth and EAPs (the oral semaglutide AUD phase 3 read out positive but modest in 2031; sNDA filed Mar 2032, decision 2033)
dementia-prevention use by 50–70-year-olds without CVD, now mostly on $49 generic semaglutide rather than tirzepatide
low-dose generic semaglutide 'maintenance microdosing' by former users trying to hold off regain
semaglutide in under-6s with monogenic or hypothalamic obesity (rare, specialist-only)
drugs.pipeline_note: FICTIONAL. The triple-agonist driver is realised as an existing product at a new dose. Lilly filed an sNDA for retatrutide 12 mg in Jun 2031 on 80-week TRIUMPH data (~28.7% mean loss). The FDA approved it in Apr 2032, restricted to BMI ≥35 with a comorbidity, with baseline DXA recommended for 60+, plus the dysesthesia, lean-mass and new NAION labelling. No new triple agonist entity launched. Amycretin was under review at the start of the step and was approved in Feb 2032 (~22% loss). Launch was muted by the Novo scandal. The under-12 driver is realised by weekly semaglutide for ages 6–11 (STEP Young), approved Oct 2031 with bone, growth and new ophthalmology postmarketing requirements. MariTide remains the only monthly product. Implants are still preclinical or phase 1, and bimagrumab-type muscle adjuncts are still in phase 3 with no filing. The US generic is semaglutide only. Tirzepatide's earliest US generic entry is mid-decade at the soonest under existing patents. The global incretin market is roughly flat at ~$135–140B. US net revenue fell ~15% in 2032 as generic semaglutide took ~55% of semaglutide prescriptions by Q4.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Still the leading cause of discontinuation. Retatrutide 12 mg has the highest early GI rates. Persistent diarrhoea in long-term users now triggers faecal elastase testing.
Elevated with rapid weight loss. Higher on retatrutide 12 mg.
Acute pancreatitis is still not causally confirmed and absolute risk is low. Reopened litigation now bundles exocrine and NAION claims, and it was in that discovery that the Novo documents surfaced.

safety_ledger.effect: Lean mass (muscle) loss and bone-density loss
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: FICTIONAL: the hip-fracture HR holds at ~1.3 in users 65+ after >2 years and ~1.45 in people who have cycled three or more times. Retatrutide 12 mg trial DXA shows lean mass at ~40% of total loss in over-60s. Fracture risk was a cited reason for the dementia sNDA complete response letter.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Class warning (Jul 2028) retained. The retatrutide 12 mg label recommends baseline DXA for 60+.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: FICTIONAL: an FDA Sentinel pooled analysis (2031) found ~1.6 cases per 10,000 person-years on drug vs ~0.7 in matched controls with obesity and diabetes. Risk is higher at high semaglutide doses and on retatrutide, and concentrated in people with a crowded optic disc, sleep apnoea or diabetes. At ~40M users that is roughly 3,500 excess cases a year, each usually permanent partial vision loss in one eye. Novo documents unsealed in Feb 2031 show a 2027 internal pooled analysis with a similar signal that was characterised in periodic reports as 'confounded by diabetes' and not submitted in full.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Class warning in Warnings and Precautions for all GLP-1-receptor-agonist-containing products (Jul 2031): discontinue on sudden vision loss and consider ophthalmic evaluation in high-risk patients. Ophthalmology postmarketing requirement added to the pediatric semaglutide approval. EMA aligned in late 2031.

safety_ledger.effect: Reward blunting / emotional flattening ('Ozempic personality', anhedonia)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: FICTIONAL: the FDA postmarketing observational study's interim analysis (2031) found clinically meaningful anhedonia at ~6–7% of users vs ~3% of controls, dose-related and highest on retatrutide (~10%). Causality still rests on observational data, with no randomised trial.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Added to Adverse Reactions class-wide in Jul 2031 as 'uncommon: decreased interest or pleasure'. No boxed or W&P warning.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Half to two-thirds regain within 18 months, worse after repeated cycles. The 2031 wave of fear-driven stops produced a visible regain cohort by late 2032, now partly re-entering on generics.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None directly; it underpins chronic-therapy framing and conditional coverage.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: B12, iron and vitamin D deficiency are common in low-intake users, and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency appears in users with EPI.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Label language added (Jul 2031) recommending periodic micronutrient assessment.

safety_ledger.effect: Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency after 5+ years of continuous use
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: FICTIONAL: further Danish and US data hold the excess at ~2× after year 5 for semaglutide. Partial recovery of faecal elastase within 6–12 months of stopping is seen in about half of cases. The tirzepatide signal is directionally similar but statistically thin.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Warnings and Precautions added for semaglutide products (Jul 2031). Class statement for others says 'data limited'. EMA PRAC concluded similarly.

safety_ledger.effect: Long-horizon effects beyond ~5 years; effects in adolescents and children on drug for decades; effects of repeated on/off cycling
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: About ten years of semaglutide follow-up now exist. Two decade-scale signals (EPI and NAION at volume) are on record. Weekly semaglutide from age 6 extends potential lifetime exposure further. Pediatric bone data from the 2029 liraglutide cohort show no deficit at 2 years, too early to matter.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Pediatric bone, growth and ophthalmology postmarketing requirements. NIH long-term cohort funding is unchanged.

safety_ledger.effect: Compounded / counterfeit / imported product harms (dosing errors, contamination, substitution)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: FICTIONAL: non-approved-product adverse-event reports grew more slowly after generic launch. ~3M gray-market users remain, concentrated on high-dose 'research' retatrutide and tirzepatide analogues. Poison-centre calls are down ~30% from their 2030 peak.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Import alert retained, serialised pens standard, and personal-importation enforcement still weak.

food_and_beverage.state: About 29% of US households now have a user, down from 33%. Snack and confectionery volumes are still ~7% below 2025, but the decline has stopped and lower-income regainers are lifting value-pack volume slightly. Premium protein lines lost some growth as top-third use fell. Unpinned-adjacent 'whole food' brands (sourdough, full-fat dairy, grass-fed) are growing fast from a small base. Protein ingredient prices have eased.

alcohol.state: US spirits volumes are ~11% below 2025 and beer ~6%. The decline slowed as fewer people took the drugs, but cheap generic semaglutide is now the default off-label tool in EAP alcohol programmes. Craft distillers keep consolidating. Non-alcoholic lines are steady.

restaurants.state: Traffic is up ~1–2% from 2030 as former users return. Casual-dining checks have recovered slightly. Small-plate menus persist, and 'full plate' and family-style concepts are back in Nashville, Boise and Denver suburbs, marketed to the unmedicated crowd. QSR value menus hold in lower-income markets.

apparel.state: Plus-size contraction has stopped and Torrid's store count is stable. Regain demand and cheaper medication cancel out. The premium tier is moving from 'structured' athleisure to heavier natural-fibre workwear aesthetics coded unmedicated. Stretch and resale serve cyclers.

fitness.state: Strength training is still growing. DXA-plus-coaching premium memberships ($250–400) are flat as top-tier users stop the drug but keep the scans. Employer metabolic tracks have dropped clinic visits for pharmacy fill checks and quarterly weigh-ins. Retatrutide 12 mg patients generate prescribed resistance-training referrals.

insurance.state: Pharmacy trend fell to ~+3% in 2032 as generic semaglutide replaced branded fills. Employer coverage rose to 41%, almost all conditional: generic-first, a ≥5% weight-loss continuation threshold, fill-data adherence and premium differentials. Prior authorisation now requires a documented eye-risk screen for retatrutide and high-dose semaglutide. Medicare Part D gross incretin spend fell ~$11B, and 2033 Part D premium bids flattened.

pharma.state: Novo is in crisis: its US semaglutide revenue was roughly halved by generics, a NAION litigation reserve is reported in the low billions, the CEO resigned in Mar 2031, and a False Claims Act qui tam suit is pending with DOJ undecided on intervening. Lilly grows on tirzepatide and retatrutide 12 mg, though its guidance was trimmed on the NAION class warning. Viatris, Teva and Sandoz gain generic volume at thin margins. Amgen's MariTide is losing clinic share to generics. Overall US incretin net revenue is down ~15%.

body_and_culture.what_the_body_signals: The signal flipped at the top. In 2030 a lean, lifted body meant covered and coached. In 2032, in the top tier, a strong body that is visibly not on anything ('born weight': broad, sunburned, a little soft at the middle, lots of muscle) is the new status, because it says you could afford the drug and chose not to. The lean, slightly depleted generic-semaglutide body now reads as lower-middle and compliant: the warehouse, the call centre, the $49 pen. A regained body over 50 still reads as lost coverage.
body_and_culture.thinness_and_class: Among upper-income mothers aged 30–49 in Nashville's Green Hills and the Denver suburbs, quitting is the story told at dinner, with the eye scare and the Novo memos as the reason. In the Columbus logistics corridor the drug is cheaper and more required than ever: coverage now depends on hitting a 5% target, and generic pens arrive by mail. Bottom-third users who once bought Indian vials on Telegram now buy the same molecule at Kroger for $49, and the gray market's social shops have moved to high-dose retatrutide.
body_and_culture.eating_as_ritual: Bread is back as a statement. Unpinned households post the 'full table' (whole loaf, butter, roast) as a visual signature. The 'Bread Alone' fasting churches (~600 congregations) and the Unpinned movement share aesthetics but argue over whether fasting is a discipline or a deprivation. Shared meals in medicated households stay short.
body_and_culture.dating_and_intimacy: Hinge and Bumble added a 'pin-free' profile badge in 2032 next to the existing 'on/off' markers. It is self-declared, with no verification. Lean-mass-verified badges are losing premium uptake. Couples where one partner quit after the vision warning report a new mismatch: one partner's appetite came back and the other's did not.
body_and_culture.meaning_of_appetite: For the Unpinned, appetite is proof of being intact, an organ that has not been bought. For conditional-coverage workers, appetite is something you manage to keep your plan. Unmuted's class argument now has a concrete target: the people being asked to medicate are the ones who cannot afford the coach and the scan that make going off safe. The MAHA wing reads the Novo memos as vindication.

interior_life.reward_blunting_prevalence_note: FICTIONAL: labelled since Jul 2031 as 'uncommon: decreased interest or pleasure'. ~6–7% of users vs ~3% of controls, up to ~10% on retatrutide. Mild 'evenness' is still widely reported but no longer marketed.
interior_life.framing: A side effect. The label line turned 'steadiness' from a selling point into a liability. HR departments removed 'even under pressure' from competency frameworks after employment lawyers began citing the label in demand letters. Clinicians now ask a two-question anhedonia screen at refill, and wellness vendors rebranded their programmes as 'metabolic health' only.
interior_life.effect_on_work: About 6M employees sit in conditional metabolic tracks, but what is verified is fills and weight, not mood. Shift-lead promotion criteria no longer mention calm. Monitoring is still deep: pharmacy fill data feed vendors under consent forms, and clinic-administered monthly dosing is fading because the generic weekly pen is cheaper. The two EEOC charges are still unresolved. Top-tier firms monitor nothing, and a growing share of their staff are off the drug.
interior_life.effect_on_art_and_play: Unmuted 'off nights' are no longer novel and have merged into ordinary loud-music bar programming in Detroit and Baltimore. The 'flat' fiction imprint folded into its parent house in 2032. Sportsbook wagering per account has recovered about a third of its decline. Unpinned has its own aesthetic of film photography, sourdough, wool and enamel pin-free badges, and its own folk-revival playlists.
interior_life.effect_on_intimacy: The labelled side effect gave couples a vocabulary: 'it's on the label' is now both reassurance and accusation in therapy rooms. Switching from monthly MariTide back to weekly generic brought weekly timing back. Drug holidays for anniversaries are common again because restarting generic is cheap.
interior_life.effect_on_politics: The Senate HELP oversight hearing on the Novo documents (Apr 2031) produced no bill. A 'Pin-Free Pledge' circulated in 2032 primaries, signed by ~40 congressional candidates, mostly MAHA-aligned Republicans plus a handful of progressive Democrats, and it promises opposition to adherence-conditioned premiums. No state or federal law changed. The medicated and the unmedicated still vote in different zip codes, but the unmedicated zip codes now include the richest ones.

state.regulatory_posture: No new state action: no new laws, mandates, coverage or premium rules. The FDA did its routine work. It approved generic semaglutide ANDAs, retatrutide 12 mg, amycretin and pediatric semaglutide, issued the July 2031 class labelling (NAION warning, anhedonia adverse reaction, EPI and micronutrient language), and issued a complete response letter on the dementia sNDA. Congress held hearings and passed nothing.
state.subsidy_or_mandate: None new. TrumpRx operates on manufacturer-set prices. The Bridge pilot was not revived. The 2027 tri-agency 30% wellness guidance stands, and employers now apply it to generic-first conditional plans.
state.conditioning_or_surveillance: Unchanged in law. In practice the conditioning moved from mood to metrics: fill data and quarterly weights decide coverage continuation in employer tracks. The same two state Medicaid programmes condition on adherence and BMI progress. Eye-screen documentation has become a new data field in prior authorisation.
state.workforce_or_military: TRICARE rules unchanged. The Army recruit oral pilot added a vision-screen step without expanding. DOT has still not ruled on drivers' alcohol-reduction use. FAA medical examiners now ask about incretin use under the NAION warning through guidance to examiners, not a rule.
state.geopolitics_of_supply: US generic semaglutide is made largely from Indian and Chinese API, so the supply chain looks like India's even when the pen is legal. US–India trade talks have dropped incretin mail enforcement as a priority. In Denmark the Novo scandal is a national economic story: the share price is roughly halved from 2030, pension funds are exposed, and the Danish FSA is investigating disclosure.

events.event: Documents unsealed in consolidated incretin litigation show Novo Nordisk's 2027 internal pooled analysis found a NAION signal it described to regulators as 'confounded by diabetes' without submitting the full analysis; Novo's CEO resigns in March, and a Senate HELP hearing follows in April

FDA adds a class-wide NAION warning to all GLP-1-receptor-agonist products after a Sentinel analysis shows ~2× risk, and in the same update labels 'decreased interest or pleasure' as an uncommon adverse reaction and adds exocrine insufficiency warnings for semaglutide
FDA approves weekly semaglutide for obesity in children aged 6–11 on STEP Young data, with bone, growth and ophthalmology postmarketing requirements

Generic semaglutide launches in the US after the compound patent expires and a November 2031 settlement clears pen patents; by summer, cash prices fall to $39–69 a month and large employers restore coverage on generic-first, 5%-target, fill-verified terms
FDA approves a 12 mg dose of Lilly's retatrutide showing ~29% average weight loss at 80 weeks, restricted to BMI 35+ with a comorbidity and carrying DXA and eye-risk guidance

The Unpinned movement's 'Pin-Free Sunday' draws an estimated 60,000 to Nashville's Centennial Park; dating apps add a 'pin-free' badge and about 40 primary candidates sign a pledge against adherence-conditioned premiums

open_tensions: The drug became cheap just as the people who could always afford it began putting it down. Generic semaglutide at $49 now flows mainly to workers whose coverage depends on hitting weight targets, while the top tier's 'born weight' aesthetic recodes their compliance as low status.

NAION, EPI, anhedonia and fracture are now all on the label of a drug that employer plans, Medicaid conditioning and pediatric approvals from age six all treat as lifelong. Each signal emerged only with years of exposure, and the cohorts that will show the next one are already enrolled.

Novo's disclosure scandal is unresolved: the qui tam suit, the Danish probe and the litigation reserve will set how much the market trusts the rest of the class's long-term safety files, including Lilly's retatrutide 12 mg, now the most efficacious and least long-studied product.

The dementia-risk extension was refused pending confirmatory data, but 50–70-year-olds are self-prescribing $49 generic semaglutide for brain protection anyway. Medicare's fracture-prone population is drifting onto the drug outside any coded, monitored route.

prose.headline: The Pen Got Cheap. The Rich Put It Down. Inside America's $49 Semaglutide Economy and the Bread-Baking Backlash
prose.world_in_600_words:
At the end of 2032 about one American adult in seven takes an incretin drug, down from nearly one in five two years ago. The drop did not come from price. It came from trust, and from Denmark. In February 2031, documents unsealed in pancreas litigation showed that Novo Nordisk's own analysts had found a signal for a rare, sudden optic-nerve stroke years earlier and had told regulators it was probably diabetes talking. That may even have been a reasonable reading. Novo kept the full analysis to itself, and that is the part people remember. The chief executive left. Senators held a hearing and passed nothing. In July the FDA put a vision warning on every drug in the class, and in the same update it wrote down two things clinicians had been saying for years: long-term semaglutide can wear down the pancreas's digestive function, and a minority of users lose some of their capacity for pleasure. The label calls it uncommon. Employers who had been writing 'steadiness' into job descriptions quietly took it out.

That summer and autumn millions stopped, most of them the longest-treated users, who were disproportionately affluent. Then the patents ran out. In January 2032 generic semaglutide reached American pharmacies, and by summer it cost less than a gym membership, $39 to $69 a month at Costco or Kroger. The pen that had cost a thousand dollars now costs about a tank of gas. Lapsed users came back, the Telegram vial trade shrank by almost half, and employers who had abandoned weight-loss coverage returned on new terms: generic first, lose five percent in six months or lose the benefit, and your fills are reported. Paying for it is no longer the obstacle. Paperwork, eye exams and an hour off work are.

The science kept moving. Lilly's retatrutide at a higher dose now takes off close to thirty percent of body weight, surgery from a pen, and it comes with instructions about bone scans and eyes. Novo's amycretin arrived and barely registered. Weekly semaglutide is now approved from age six, and close to a million children take an incretin drug. The FDA turned down Lilly's request to market tirzepatide for dementia prevention to older adults without heart disease. Many of those adults now buy the generic anyway.

The culture turned over at the top. In Nashville's Green Hills and the Denver suburbs, mothers in their thirties and forties tell quitting stories at dinner. A movement called Unpinned gives it a look of whole loaves, full-fat butter, wool, film cameras and a white enamel badge. Its members call their bodies 'born weight': broad, strong, a little soft. In June, sixty thousand people filled a Nashville park for a 'Pin-Free Sunday'. Dating apps added a badge for it. About forty primary candidates signed a pledge against tying insurance premiums to adherence. No law changed.

Further down the income ladder, the generic body is the job body. In the Columbus logistics corridor and in call centres in Texas, coverage is a monthly number on a weigh-in sheet. The drug costs almost nothing there and is close to required. A lean, slightly depleted frame now reads as compliant rather than rich. Regainers over fifty are still the most visible group in poor neighbourhoods, and a growing share of them are re-entering at $49.

The industries have adapted rather than broken. Snack volumes stopped falling, restaurants serve family-style platters again in the suburbs where Unpinned is strong, and Novo's American business has roughly halved. From the outside the country looks nearly as thin as before and a little less calm. The drugs are cheap now, and the people who could always afford them are the ones stopping.
prose.a_day_in_the_life:
Renee Kowalczyk, fifty-one, home health aide, Toledo, picks up her pen at the Kroger on Monroe Street after a double. Forty-nine dollars on her debit card. The pharmacist slides a laminated card across with it: SUDDEN BLURRING IN ONE EYE — STOP, CALL. She already has two at home.

In the car she checks the box out of habit, holding it to the dome light for the serial code she used to look for on the vials from Hyderabad. This one has no code to check. It just says semaglutide.

She stopped last August, the week the news said 'optic nerve'. She ate toast standing up for four months, and she knows what the scale said. Her client, Mr. Abernathy, ninety, told her she looked healthier. She did not take it as a compliment.

At home her daughter Kayla, twenty-four, is on FaceTime from Nashville, where she nannies for a family in Green Hills. The mother there quit everything, Kayla says, and bakes now. There's a pin. Kayla holds it up: white enamel, a pen with a line through it.

'You'd look cute in it,' Renee says.

'I'm not on anything, Mom. That's the point.'

Renee lays the pen on the counter next to the ophthalmology referral she hasn't scheduled. The appointment is in Perrysburg, a Tuesday, unpaid. She picks the pen up and sets it down again.

Kayla is showing her a loaf of bread, heavy and split along the top. Renee says it looks beautiful, and she means it, and she can smell nothing through the phone. She uncaps the pen, finds the soft place beside her navel, and counts to six while Kayla talks about the butter.
